hook:
The $20 all-you-can-eat AI editor is gone.
Cursor and GitHub Copilot are now agent-first and credit-metered,
with entry tiers that deliberately restrict models or features.

sections.title: Your editor budget now buys a different contract
sections.content:
If your renewal approval still assumes bundled model choice, the old editor budget is misleading.

Choose by model dependence and review workflow, not completion quality. The bill follows that choice.

> Evidence: vendor pricing and acquisition documents, verified 10 November 2026; no independent performance measurements.

Cursor's ownership changed before this renewal decision. The acquisition is complete, not an option still awaiting exercise.

- 21 April 2026: SpaceX and Cursor announced a partnership with a $10B payment and a $60B acquisition option.
- 16 June 2026: SpaceX signed the all-stock deal at a $60B valuation, through X67 Inc.
- 14 August 2026: the deal closed; Cursor joined SpaceXAI to work on Grok, Grok Build, Grok Bot and Cursor.

> Cursor states its constraint was compute: “We've wanted to push our training efforts much further, but we've been bottlenecked by compute.”

sections.title: Model ownership and repository ownership impose different limits
sections.content:
Cursor's philosophy: the model is the product, so the editor must own the model and the inference bill. That rules out treating cheap access as a neutral model buffet.

- Cursor states that Plus offers only Grok models; Premium opens third-party access, not an included third-party allowance.

GitHub's philosophy: the repository is the product, so AI must land in review, PRs and issues. That rules out treating the editor as an isolated purchase.

- GitHub's paid review and cloud-assignment gates make repository work part of the buying decision.

These are business constraints, not claims that either tool cannot edit code. Start with what each contract refuses to bundle; the feature checklist comes later.

sections.title: The meters punish different habits
sections.content:
Read these prices as penalties. Cursor punishes heavy third-party use and rewards Grok loyalty; Copilot punishes agent breadth across seats and rewards staying inside GitHub's surfaces.

| Vendor's monthly offer | Usage that incurs the penalty |
|---|---|
| Cursor: $8 Plus; $30 Premium | Plus is Grok-only; Premium is the first third-party tier, at API list price on top |
| GitHub Copilot: $10 Pro with $15 GitHub AI Credits; $39 Pro+; $100 Max | Agent mode, review, cloud, CLI and app consume the same credit meter |

Third-party usage is outside Cursor's monthly price. GitHub's meter spans activities; changing surfaces does not escape it.

| Pro scenario (hypothetical) | Subscription floor |
|---|---|
| Small: 10 users | $10/user/month × 10 users = $100/month |
| Growing: 30 users | $10/user/month × 30 users = $300/month |

> Subscription arithmetic only. Extra Copilot credits cost more; neither seat count predicts agent consumption.

sections.title: Model neutrality now needs a renewal check
sections.content:
Teams that chose Cursor partly to stay model-agnostic now buy from a company whose model is Grok. Ownership changed the incentive. It does not prove that every request routes to Grok.

> Default routing is a renewal risk to inspect, not an observed routing result in this comparison.

Before renewing, replay representative repository tasks and record the selected model, any routing changes and the separately billed third-party usage. Keep the outputs for review.

- Compare the model you requested with the model actually used.
- Have reviewers judge the resulting changes, not the subscription label.
- Do not buy Plus if non-Grok access is a requirement; test Premium's unbundled bill before committing.

sections.title: Copilot Free is a working entry point, not the review tier
sections.content:
GitHub's counter-argument is distribution, not model neutrality. Copilot Free already supports agent mode and the CLI, with limited usage. It is not a no-agent demo.

- Free can exercise the local agent workflow before a subscription decision.
- PR review, file diff review and custom instructions start at Pro.
- Assigning work to Copilot so it creates a pull request also starts at Pro.

The boundary is concrete. A successful CLI trial does not establish that Free can perform your review workflow.

> Pro buys access to repository-side work, not an unlimited agent budget.

Do not choose Free for a process that requires those paid gates. Try the actual handoff from assigned work to reviewed PR before migrating the team.

sections.title: Choose Grok commitment or repository consolidation today
sections.content:
Grok-committed editor buyers and GitHub review-centric teams should choose Cursor and GitHub Copilot, respectively. Buy the constraint you can accept.

- Choose Cursor if Grok meets your workload and third-party usage is optional, with a separate budget when needed.
- Choose GitHub Copilot if review and assigned PR work matter more than owning a separate editor workflow.

Switching changes more than the invoice. Inventory model assumptions and review handoffs before moving; a subscription change is not a workflow migration.

> If your hard requirement is a fixed fee covering heavy third-party use, neither published offer establishes that contract. Stay put rather than assume it.

Today, bring a representative change to review and inspect its model choice and billed usage before approving renewal.

decision_matrix.situation: Grok meets the workload and third-party access is unnecessary
decision_matrix.why: Plus's Grok-only restriction matches the requirement rather than obstructing it.

decision_matrix.situation: Reviews and assigned PR work belong in the existing GitHub process
decision_matrix.why: Pro opens those repository-side workflows under the same credit meter.

decision_matrix.situation: A free trial must include an agent and CLI, but not PR review
decision_matrix.why: Free supports both surfaces with limited usage.

decision_matrix.situation: The budget must include PR review without a paid subscription
decision_matrix.why: Copilot gates PR review at Pro and Cursor lists Bugbot under Premium.

decision_matrix.situation: Heavy third-party usage must fit a fixed subscription fee
decision_matrix.why: Cursor excludes those tokens from the subscription and Copilot's credits remain metered.

decision_matrix.situation: An existing Cursor team requires model neutrality at renewal
decision_matrix.pick: Cursor — only after a routing check
decision_matrix.why: Ownership now favors Grok, so the team must verify model selection and the separate third-party bill.

decision_matrix.situation: A Copilot rollout will add seats and agent surfaces together
decision_matrix.pick: GitHub Copilot — after a usage trial
decision_matrix.why: Seat arithmetic establishes only the subscription floor, not consumption across the shared meter.

cost_math.label: Hypothetical small team: Copilot Pro subscription floor
Hypothetical growing team: Copilot Pro subscription floor

verdict_summary: Grok-committed editor buyers should choose Cursor; GitHub review-centric teams should choose GitHub Copilot Pro or above. Before renewing, inspect model routing and separately billed usage for Cursor, or trial the review handoff and shared credit consumption for Copilot.

faqs.q: Does Copilot require moving to a particular editor?
faqs.a: GitHub lists support for VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains, Xcode, Eclipse, Neovim and Zed, among other surfaces. GitHub Mobile is also supported.

faqs.q: What else does Cursor Premium bundle?
faqs.a: Cursor lists code hosting through Origin and AI code reviews through Bugbot, alongside cloud agents and automations.

faqs.q: What do Cursor's higher individual tiers advertise?
faqs.a: Cursor lists Super at $100/month with 15× Plus usage and priority model access at peak times. Ultra is $200/month with 50× Plus usage and earliest access to all products and models.

faqs.q: What distinguishes Copilot Pro+ beyond its subscription price?
faqs.a: GitHub lists $70/month in total credits, premium models including Opus, and audit logs for Pro+.
